prompt: Put the steps of handling a client change request in order.

task.prompt: Put the steps of handling a client change request in order.

items.label: Log the request with the client's description and date
Assess impact on scope, schedule, cost and risk with the team
Send the client the impact and options
Get written approval or rejection from the authorised client contact
Update the plan, backlog and change log

task.explanation: Log first so nothing is lost; assess before quoting; decide with the authorised person; only then change the baseline.

prompt: Write the summary section of a change request for the client, based on the context. Keep it factual and decision-ready.

task.prompt: Write the summary section of a change request for the client, based on the context. Keep it factual and decision-ready.
task.context: Project: fixed-price white-label fitness app, launch 30 June. The client's head of marketing asked on a call (3 May) to add Apple Health and Google Fit sync. The team estimates 70 hours (rate $90/h = $6,300) and 1.5 weeks of extra calendar time because both integrations need store-review permission changes. Option B: ship Apple Health only for launch (40 hours, $3,600, no date change) and add Google Fit in the next release.

rubric.label: What and why
rubric.description: States the requested change, who asked and when, without editorialising.

rubric.label: Impact
rubric.description: Gives cost, effort and schedule impact with the figures from the context.

rubric.label: Options
rubric.description: Presents both options clearly so the client can choose.

rubric.label: Decision needed
rubric.description: Asks for a decision by a date from the authorised approver, and says nothing changes until approval.

task.sampleAnswer:
Change request CR-07: health-data sync

Request: On 3 May, the head of marketing asked to add Apple Health and Google Fit sync to the launch scope.

Impact:
- Option A (both integrations): 70 hours, $6,300. Launch moves from 30 June to about 10 July, because both need store-review permission changes.
- Option B (Apple Health only at launch): 40 hours, $3,600. Launch stays 30 June; Google Fit follows in the next release (estimated separately).

Decision needed: please confirm Option A, Option B or no change by 10 May, approved by the project sponsor. Until then the current plan and launch date stand.

prompt: A junior PM wrote this change request. Mark the lines that make it weak or risky.

task.prompt: A junior PM wrote this change request. Mark the lines that make it weak or risky.

segments.text: CR-12: add a referral programme to the customer app.
Requested by: the client's marketing team.
segments.issue: No named requester or date; the decision trail needs a person.

segments.text: Estimate: should be fine, the team thinks it's small.
segments.issue: No hours, cost or schedule impact; the client cannot decide on "small".

segments.text: Impact on launch date: none, we will work faster.
segments.issue: Assumes extra speed instead of assessing the real schedule impact.

segments.text: Dependencies: requires a promo-code service already in scope.
Approval: approved verbally by the client's intern on Slack.
segments.issue: Approval must come from the contractually authorised contact, in writing.

segments.text: Acceptance criteria: referrer and referee each get a $5 credit after the referee's first order.
Risk: referral fraud; mitigation is one credit per device and payment card.

prompt: A client asks for "a small tweak": the AI meal planner should also handle allergies. The team says that means a new data model, prompt changes and a fresh evaluation set, about 2 sprints. The contract is fixed-price with a change-control clause.

task.prompt: A client asks for "a small tweak": the AI meal planner should also handle allergies. The team says that means a new data model, prompt changes and a fresh evaluation set, about 2 sprints. The contract is fixed-price with a change-control clause.

steps.question: What do you do first?
options: Log it as a change request and assess impact with the team
Agree on the call since it sounds small
Tell the client it is impossible
Ask the team to fit it in the current sprint
steps.explanation: Changes go through the agreed process before anyone commits to them.

steps.question: The client says it should have been obvious and refuses to pay. What is your next move?
options: Walk through the signed scope and acceptance criteria with them, and offer options: pay, swap out equal scope, or defer
Do it free to keep the relationship
Stop all work until they pay
Escalate straight to lawyers
steps.explanation: The baseline settles what was agreed; options keep the relationship constructive.

steps.question: They choose to swap out an equal-sized feature. What must happen next?
options: Nothing, since cost is unchanged
Record the swap as an approved change with the removed scope named, and update plan and acceptance criteria
Update the backlog only
Mention it in the next status report
steps.explanation: Zero-cost swaps are still changes; without a record the removed feature returns at UAT as a dispute.

prompt: Five change requests are waiting. You can assess two this week. Rank them, most urgent first.

task.prompt: Five change requests are waiting. You can assess two this week. Rank them, most urgent first.

items.label: Legal requires a cookie-consent change before a launch in 10 days
Payment provider deprecates the API version the app uses in 6 weeks
Client wants a new onboarding flow for a campaign in 2 months
Sales asked for a demo-only feature for a prospect, no date
Designer suggests a new icon set

task.explanation: Legal and deadline-driven changes first, then externally forced technical change, then dated business requests; undated nice-to-haves last.

prompt: Who should approve a change request that increases the price of a fixed-bid project?

options: Any client stakeholder who attends the sprint review
The agency's tech lead
The client contact authorised in the contract to approve changes
The PM, if the change is under 10% of the budget
mcq.explanation: Commercial changes need an authorised approver; otherwise the agency risks unpaid work and disputes.

prompt: Why keep a change log even for rejected change requests?

options: Rejected requests can be billed later
It shows the client what was asked and decided, which prevents the same item reappearing as a dispute later
It is required for every project by law
It improves velocity
mcq.explanation: The decision trail protects both sides. Rejected items are often re-raised at UAT as "we always expected that".

prompt: On a T&M project with a monthly cap, the client keeps adding stories. What is the role of change control here?

options: None; T&M projects have no change control
Refusing all new stories
Showing how new work affects the cap and the forecast end date, so the client can decide what to trade
Billing each new story separately
mcq.explanation: T&M shifts cost risk to the client but the client still needs to see the effect on the cap and the date to decide.
